key_insight: Parents and pediatric clinicians were more willing to use AI when the condition seemed more serious, but trust dropped when data sharing expanded or AI and clinicians disagreed.
clinical_relevance: For pediatric settings, AI adoption is likely to depend on clear privacy safeguards, transparent performance, and how well AI is framed for diagnosis versus treatment decisions.
method: Surveyed parents across two cohorts (n=198 and n=79) and pediatric healthcare professionals (n=33).
Compared willingness to use AI across disease, diagnosis, and treatment scenarios, including cases where AI and clinician recommendations conflicted.
Examined predictors such as data privacy, AI knowledge, and perceived disease severity.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports significant associations, including reduced willingness with broader data sharing (p < .001) and higher willingness when perceived disease severity was greater in one parent cohort (β = .10, p = .013).
watch_item: Results reflect stated preferences, not real-world outcomes, so implementation should be cautious about overgeneralizing to actual clinical decisions.
paper_title: Acceptability of AI-applications in routine clinical care for children and adolescents: perspectives of parents and healthcare professionals
